title: ‘The Light in the Darkness’ Holocaust-Narrative Game Launches ‘Director’s Cut’ Version (Gaming News Roundup)
description:
“The Light in the Darkness: Director’s Cut,” from game designer Luc Bernard, launched Tuesday.

	Originally released in 2023, the free Holocaust nar
body:
“The Light in the Darkness: Director’s Cut,” from game designer Luc Bernard, launched Tuesday.

	Originally released in 2023, the free Holocaust narrative game puts players in the experience of a Polish-Jewish family in Nazi-occupied France. This newly expanded and enhanced edition features fully voiced scenes, extended narrative content, refined visuals and updated gameplay systems.


	The game is published by Voices of the Forgotten, Bernard’s nonprofit dedicated to promoting Holocaust education through digital media. In August 2023, a virtual Holocaust Museum designed by Bernard became available in the Fortnite Creative video game.
	

	“The Light in the Darkness: Director’s Cut” is available now on PlayStation 5.


	See more gaming news from the week in the roundup below.
	
		PARTNERSHIPS/COLLABS	

	“KPop Demon Hunters” and “Ghostbusters” join “Monopoly Go!” in the mobile game’s new “Monster Mash” season.

	From Sept. 23-Nov. 25, “Monopoly Go!” players can experience a spooky season as the “KPop Demon Hunters” and “Ghostbusters” franchises take over the game with HUNTR/X, the Saja Boys, the Ghostbusters crew and more.

	For the first time, “Monopoly Go!” will feature hit songs, with “Golden” and “How It’s Done” from “KPop Demon Hunters” available in game. “Ghostbusters” comes to life in the game with themed vehicles, attractions and iconic ghost-busting equipment.

	Monster Mash also introduces the Luck-O-Lantern, which unlocks rewards when filled with enough candy, and a dice duel with friends where each roll reveals a trick or a treat. There are 25 new Sticker Sets hidden throughout the game.
	
	
		GAME UPDATES/DLC	

	“The Sims 4” released an update featuring new ways to style young Sims’ looks and spaces.

	Available now, the free update features one new hairstyle, three adult hairstyles now available for kids and three new CAS assets for toddlers. Also available are six new Styled Looks, eight new Build/Buy items, a new Styled Room and seven new Sims joining the Gallery.

	Per EA, “The Sims” will continue to release free content updates throughout the year.

schema.headline: ‘The Light in the Darkness’ Holocaust-Narrative Game Launches ‘Director’s Cut’ Version (Gaming News Roundup)

body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	The hottest ticket in New York City is to the Knicks home opener at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, Oct. 20. Since winning the NBA Finals against the San Antonio Spurs back in June, the Knicks have become the toast of New York with good vibes around the city, massive TV ratings and even Jalen Brunson hosting the premiere episode of “Saturday Night Live.”

	The home opener for the Knicks just isn’t the first game of the 2026-2027 season, but it’s also when the team gets to raise their championship banner in MSG and the players get their championship rings. In addition, this is the first championship ceremony for the Knicks since 1973 — that’s 53 years without a banner. It’s a historic event in the NBA and no Knicks fan should miss it.


	However, with pricing difficulties that led the organization to pause ticket sales temporarily, tickets to the home opener are very much sought-after and tough to get. Plus, the NBA scheduled the first game of the season against the new hot team in the league, the new look Philadelphia 76ers with the addition of former-Boston Celtic Jaylen Brown and former-L.A. Laker LeBron James joining the squad.

	Meanwhile, the Knicks resurgence in New York has attracted a slew of attention from celebrities and sports fans alike, drawing in the likes of Spike Lee, Timothee Chalamet, Kylie Jenner, Tracy Morgan, Ben Stiller, Taylor Swift, Este and Alana Haim, Mariska Hargitay and others.

	Tickets for the game, which is completely sold out, can still be found on third-party tickets sites, such as Ticketmaster, StubHub, Vivid Seats and others. Plus, hotel rooms in New York are available, including hotels near MSG, on TripAdvisor, Hotels.com, Expedia, Kayak and other booking platforms.


	Below, check out some of the best places to buy tickets for the Knicks home opener, below:


						
			
	

					Ticketmaster
	
					

	Ticketmaster has tickets to the MSG home opener: Philadelphia 76ers vs. New York Knicks. The retailer is the official ticket seller of the pro league, so one of the best ways to buy and sell NBA tickets is through Ticketmaster.


						
			
	

					StubHub
	
					

	We found tickets for Philadelphia 76ers vs. New York Knicks at the resale site StubHub starting at $1,057 for two tickets, at the time of publishing. We like the retailer because of their “FanProtect Guarantee,” which means all tickets sold are authentic, valid and delivered to your email inbox before tipoff.

	In fact, StubHub goes further with customer service. If your event is canceled and not rescheduled for a later date, the retailer says you’ll receive 120% in credit, or a full refund without the extra 20%.


						
			
	

					Vivid Seats
	
					

	76ers vs. Knicks tickets are still available starting at $1,008 for two tickets at Vivid Seats, at the time of publishing. Plus, if you sign up for the retailer’s newsletter, you’ll get 10% off your first purchase — which makes tickets even cheaper.


			
			
			
			
	

					SeatGeek
	
					

	For tickets to Philadelphia vs. New York, SeatGeek is another great resource with prices starting at $1,025 for two tickets, at the time of this writing. As a bonus, you can use promo code VARIETY10 to save $10 for cheaper tickets at SeatGeek.com.


			
			
			
			
	

					Ticket Network
	
					

	With prices starting at $1,274 for two, TicketNetwork has tickets for Philadelphia 76ers vs. New York Knicks home opener at MSG. The resale platform also has tickets available for purchase. You can save $150 off when you spend $500 with promo code VARIETY150, or $300 off when you spend $1,000 with promo code VARIETY300 at TicketNetwork.com.

	If you’re unable to attend the game in-person, you can watch all of the hoops action during the Knicks home opener on NBC. The broadcast network is available to watch for free with DirecTV, Fubo, Hulu + Live TV, Peacock and others.

title: RioFilme to Announce $20 Million Film and TV Incentives at Rio Film Fest’s RioMarket
description: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — RioFilme, the film and TV company of Rio de Janeiro City, will launch a call for proposals amounting to R$100 million ($20
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — RioFilme, the film and TV company of Rio de Janeiro City, will launch a call for proposals amounting to R$100 million ($20 million) for film and TV show production, development, distribution and international co-productions, Leonardo Edde, president of RioFilme, told Variety.

	RioFilme will unveil Oct. 1 the incentive package, the largest one of the company this year, during the first day of RioMarket, the business section of the Rio International Film Fest, Edde said.
	

	The incentive package is composed of six lines. The main one will support at least 20 feature fiction and animation film productions, which will divide $10.4 million, while a line totaling $2 million will fund the production of at least three live-action fiction and animated series.


	A minimum of 12 documentary productions, including theatrical, TV or streaming works, will receive a total of $2.4 million. A further $1 million in development funding will be available to 20 projects for cinema, TV and streaming, while a total of $1.2 million is destined to fund the distribution of a minimum of 12 feature films.

	The novelty of this year’s incentive package, said Edde, is a $3 million line for at least four international co-production projects of fiction and animated feature films.

	The first five lines are for productions in which a Rio-based company is the leading producer, he added. For the co-production line, however, projects in which local companies have a minority stake are also eligible, Edde stressed.

	The co-production funding is part of a plan to consolidate Rio as a major world film and TV production hub. Rio has streamlined its film commission and created incentives that has made it one of the most filmed cities in the world, surpassing Paris and Mexico City in terms of days shot in the city. In the first half of 2026, Rio hosted 40 international productions, up from 28 in the same period last year, Edde added.
	

	Companies will be able to apply for the incentives as of Out. 2. RioFilme’s selection process will take place in the fourth quarter of this year, and the coin is due to be available in the beginning of 2027.

	Fundo Setorial do Audiovisual (FSA) will provide the money for the $20 million incentive package as part of an agreement between RioFilm and the National Cinema Agency (Ancine), which manages FSA. It is the second time RioFilm and Ancine cooperate to decentralize the distribution of FSA’s funds. Last year, RioFilme also held a $20 million call for proposals, the difference being it did not include a line for international co-productions.

	“The regional arrangement is interesting because it decentralizes decisions about how and where to invest,” Edde said. “Local territories obviously understand their own strengths and potential much better than the federal government does. I strongly support this mechanism because it broadens the distribution of responsibilities and gives local territories responsibility for implementing the resources.”

	As part of the RioFilme/Ancine agreement, RioFilme is required to provide a counterpart contribution of one-third of Ancine’s total investment. RioFilme has already fulfilled the counterpart with two incentive programs this year totaling $6.6 million, Edde said.

schema.headline: RioFilme to Announce $20 Million Film and TV Incentives at Rio Film Fest’s RioMarket

title: Patti LaBelle, Common, Public Enemy Honored at Black Music Action Coalition Gala 2026
description: Patti LaBelle, Common and Public Enemy were among the artists and executives who were celebrated on Thursday night at the sixth annual Black Music A
body:
Patti LaBelle, Common and Public Enemy were among the artists and executives who were celebrated on Thursday night at the sixth annual Black Music Action Coalition Gala, held at the Beverly Hilton Hotel in Los Angeles.

	Throughout the evening, BMAC and its president/CEO Willie “Prophet” Stiggers recognized key figures in the music industry who have wielded their influence for good while amplifying the goals and accomplishments of the organization. Kenny Burns returned as a host for the sixth year, keeping the night moving while the house band 1500 or Nothin provided tunes.
	

	LaBelle was one of the stars of the evening as the recipient of the BMAC Icon Award. R&B singer Chanté Moore paid tribute to LaBelle with a rendition of “Love, Need and Want You,” followed by an impassioned, church-reared performance of “You Are My Friend” from Le’Andria Johnson, who waded into the audience to duet with LaBelle.


	Director Lee Daniels took the podium to dedicate the Icon Award to LaBelle, sharing how her presence in his life helped him overcome his battle with addiction. “Your voice is healing. Your voice is power, your voice is soul,” he said. “When I first heard your music, I was 22 years old. It changed my life, and I knew I wanted to be an artist.”


	LaBelle then thanked BMAC and shared how grateful she was to be honored at the age of 82. “I want you to know that music is medicine,” she said. “We all need that medicine, especially now that we’re going through all these trying times. Music is my life, and music will heal us all. And thank God we’re all here and that we all woke up this morning.”
	

	One of the more emotional moments of the evening came when Dr. Mahalia Hines introduced her son, rapper Common, who received the Harry Belafonte Change Agent Award. She commended him for his activism and willingness to perform concerts and hold conversations with incarcerated individuals across the United States.

	“‘What are you willing to die for? Live for that,'” Common said, recalling the words that Ambassador Andrew Young shared with him and the cast on the set of “Selma.” “That day, I went home thinking I’ve been doing activist work, but I ain’t doing any of that. Am I living for it each and every day? That made me want to improve, grow, learn and figure out ways I can improve our communities in ways that I never thought of.”

	Additional figures and organizations honored throughout the evening included Public Enemy, who was presented with the Social Impact Award by Big Daddy Kane; the Team’s Lee Anderson, Marty Diamond, Lenore Kinder, Kevin Shivers and Mallory Smith, who was given the BMAC Founders Award by Tennessee State University alumna Jamea Kollie; Nicole Wyskoarko, who received the inaugural Sylvia Rhone Visionary Award as presented by Rhone; the Universal Music Group Global Impact team, who was given the BMAC 365 Award by R&B group Flo; and Tina Davis, who was given the BMAC Clarence Avant Trailblazer Award by Montell Jordan.

schema.headline: Patti LaBelle, Common, Public Enemy Honored at Black Music Action Coalition Gala 2026

title: Fox News Assigns Larry Kudlow to Anchor Maria Bartiromo’s ‘Sunday Morning Futures’ Through Midterms
description: Fox News is replacing one opinionated business anchor with another, assigning Larry Kudlow to anchor “Sunday Morning Futures” on an interim basis fo
body:
Fox News is replacing one opinionated business anchor with another, assigning Larry Kudlow to anchor “Sunday Morning Futures” on an interim basis following its ouster of longtime staffer Maria Bartiromo.

	Kudlow will host the 10 a.m. program starting Sunday, and continue through the weekend after the midterm elections on November 8. Fox News Channel says a new host will be named at a later date.


	Kudlow, a longtime CNBC personality who joined Fox Business Network in 2021 following a stint in the first Trump administration, held several top Wall Street jobs and advised politicians ranging from President Ronald Regan to former New Jersey Governor Christine Todd Whitman on the economy from behind the scenes. On CNBC, he often held forth with another longtime host, former hedge fund manager Jim Cramer.
	

	Kudlow will take the reins of a program that was built around Bartiromo, who aimed to bring market perspective to politics, but became known for giving conservative lawmakers and officials free rein to speak their piece without being challenged overmuch on the facts. Bartiromo has not been seen on any Fox News properties since August 9, when she did what became her final broadcast of Fox Business’ “Mornings with Maria.”

	Bartiromo is believed to have passed along a directive issued to executive producers at Fox Business Network to the White House, according to a person familiar with the matter, and those instructions may have cautioned Fox Business staffers against support to outlandish claims made by President Donald Trump in public remarks. Divulging confidential company information to an outside party would likely be seen as a violation of terms of employment. An attorney for Bartiromo, Bryan Freedman, issued a statement saying Bartiromo continues to be employed by Fox News Media, but she has not been seen on its platforms in weeks.
	

	Kudlow’s eponymously titled Fox Business program Kudlow’s is the most-watched program on the cable network. He has interviewed many key newsmakers, including President Donald Trump, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Elon Musk and House Speaker Rep. Mike Johnson.

	In the past, Kudlow expressed a desire to stick to business and policy. “I like people to be able to spend their own money,” he told Variety in 2021. “I like them to have as much freedom as possible.”

schema.headline: Fox News Assigns Larry Kudlow to Anchor Maria Bartiromo’s ‘Sunday Morning Futures’ Through Midterms

title: Peter Sarsgaard Joins Kenneth Branagh in Paramount+ Series ‘Laird’
description:
Peter Sarsgaard has joined the upcoming Paramount+ drama series “Laird,” Variety has learned. 

	Sarsgaard will join previously announced lead Kenne
body:
Peter Sarsgaard has joined the upcoming Paramount+ drama series “Laird,” Variety has learned. 

	Sarsgaard will join previously announced lead Kenneth Branagh in the show, which was announced with a series order back in July. 

	The logline for “Laird” states that it is “an epic family saga in which a proud Scot defies a shadowy American billionaire (Sarsgaard) hellbent on buying up the glens. Amidst family feuds, buried secrets and star-crossed romances, the Laird of Castle Drummoch (Branagh) remains determined to protect his ancestral lands from oligarchical land grabbing.” 
	

	Sarsgaard’s character is named Peter Bergstrom, who is further described as “a ruthless, self-made tech titan and land magnate whose influence spans continents. He is not simply building wealth, but power – shaping land, industry, and people as extensions of his ambition.” 

	This will not be Sarsgaard’s first series at Paramount+. He previously starred in the series “Interrogation” when the streamer was known as CBS All Access. Sarsgaard is a two-time Emmy nominee — first for his role in the Hulu limited series “Dopesick” and then for his role in the first season of the Apple TV series “Presumed Innocent.” His other TV credits include “DTF St. Louis,” “The Looming Tower,” and “The Slap.” He is also known for roles in films like “Blue Jasmine,” “An Education,” “Kinsey,” “Jarhead,” and “Shattered Glass.” 

	He is repped by WME, ID PR, and Peikoff/Mahan. 

	“Laird” hails from Jez Butterworth and John-Henry Butterworth, the co-creators of fellow Paramount+ series “The Agency.” Jez is also the co-creator and showrunner of Paramount+’s “Mobland.” Georgia Lee is also a co-creator on “Laird.” Both the Butterworths are executive producers on “Laird,” with Branagh also executive producing in addition to starring. David Glasser, Joe Wright, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari, Charles Finch, and Keith Cox also executive produce, with Wright also attached to direct the pilot. Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios produce.

schema.headline: Peter Sarsgaard Joins Kenneth Branagh in Paramount+ Series ‘Laird’

title: ‘Charlie Harper’ Review: Emilia Jones and Nick Robinson Come Apart, in Fits and Starts, in a Fuzzy, Non-Linear Breakup Drama
description: The first thing to know about “Charlie Harper” is that it’s not, in fact, about someone called Charlie Harper. Charlie (Nick Robinson) and Harper (E
body:
The first thing to know about “Charlie Harper” is that it’s not, in fact, about someone called Charlie Harper. Charlie (Nick Robinson) and Harper (Emilia Jones) are a couple, meeting and parting at various stages across a five-year timeline; the title of this earnestly melancholy first feature by directing duo Mac Eldridge and Tom Dean implies that they’re two halves of a shared soul, whether they’re together or not. That’s one romantic notion of many in a free-floating relationship drama, which employs an intuitively non-linear structure to enliven what is otherwise a fairly conventional, ordinary love story between two attractive but imperfect people. Robinson and Jones are a likable enough pairing to make “Charlie Harper” affecting here and there; making it interesting is a taller order.
	

	Shortly after its premiere at last year’s Toronto Film Festival, “Charlie Harper” was acquired for North America by then brand-new distributor Row K Entertainment; only now, over a year later, is it hitting theaters. That delay is sort of fitting for a story largely about the time it takes for life to fall into place, but the film itself doesn’t inspire much urgency. Likelier to be found by audiences on VOD, it zigzags with some grace between the peaks and troughs of the romance at its center, but never gathers much momentum or even much depth of emotion; we surmise well before the end that our lovers probably aren’t meant to be, and for that we may feel some wistful, knowing sadness. But our hearts don’t break for them.


	We begin, naturally, somewhere in the middle: Our introduction to the principals is not theirs to each other. When Charlie approaches Harper in a low-lit bar to introduce himself, she says they’ve met before, jogging his memory about their first encounter way back in high school. But this is just another round of a game they’ve played before, with the shoe on the other foot, and when we circle back to that same scene toward the close, we’re more conscious of the weight of what has transpired between them. Starting over as strangers would be sweeter and easier. 
	

	Soon after, but several years earlier, a mirror image of this scene sees Harper taunt Charlie with feigned unfamiliarity at a college party on the night of Barack Obama’s first presidential victory: A shared backstory, more youthful still, emerges, as does a history of relationship-defining songs, exchanged on quaintly physical formats. (Their signature number is Brenda Lee’s bittersweet “Break It to Me Gently” — how happy can any romance be when it’s founded on a ballad that heartsore?) He’s a charismatic slacker, bright but aimless, and content to work menial jobs until, well, his discontent gets the better of him. She, by contrast, has a clear direction in life — from their small town to New Orleans, where she plans to train as a chef. (That makes “Charlie Harper” the second romance this year, after Netflix’s “Voicemails for Isabelle,” to pair Robinson with a gourmet love interest. Not a bad type to have.)

	For a time, they live together in shabby-chic Louisiana bliss, but the fault lines are easy to spot: Her ambitions curve ever farther away from his, and his growing drinking problem worsens matters. The film would have us believe that Charlie is a genius squandering his brilliance, though the script’s rather tenuous demonstration of this is the fact that he associates madeleines with Proust; either way, the longer we spend bouncing around their relationship, the more we sense that the couple aren’t especially compatible in their respective gifts, much less their failings.

	“Charlie Harper” is constructed with care: Eldridge and Dean’s direction can be nimble and imaginative, making up for shortfalls in the writing (by Dean alone). Sharone Meir’s lensing deftly marks the various passages of the couple’s story with clear shifts in palette and texture, from the flushed, saturated lighting of first love to the crisper, brighter clarity that comes with time and age and disappointment. Sam Levy’s editing likewise darts associatively between these moods, seemingly letting sense memory shape the chronology of proceedings. But it can feel like quite a lot of formal business for a story this slight. As viewers navigate the film’s loops and reversals, they may feel — rather like the embattled lovers working away at their relationship — that they’re putting more into this thing than they’re getting out of it.

schema.headline: ‘Charlie Harper’ Review: Emilia Jones and Nick Robinson Come Apart, in Fits and Starts, in a Fuzzy, Non-Linear Breakup Drama

title: John Cho’s Odyssey From ‘MILF Guy #2’ to Porn-Hating Pastor in ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’: ‘It Felt Very Lonesome at Times’
description:
“I’m still trying to act, and I want to be better,” offers John Cho. “And you can’t be better without a good role.”

	Cho, 54, has been fighting for
body:
“I’m still trying to act, and I want to be better,” offers John Cho. “And you can’t be better without a good role.”

	Cho, 54, has been fighting for the right roles since he first gained notice as a high school party boy chanting “MILF!” in the coming-of-age hit “American Pie” (he was credited as “MILF Guy #2). Meatier turns followed in the Chris Rock vehicle “Down to Earth” and Justin Lin’s radical indie “Better Luck Tomorrow” before he took the lead in cult favorite “Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle.” He earned critical raves as helmsman Hikaru Sulu in J.J. Abrams’ “Star Trek” films and became the first Asian American actor to topline a Hollywood thriller in 2018’s “Searching.”
	

	As a Korean American, Cho was subjected to racist typecasting early on in his career, and a humiliating moment while playing a Chinese delivery boy on “The Jeff Foxworthy Show” opened his eyes to just how bad it can get. Though he’s remained steadily employed, it’s been a constant battle for Cho to find exciting parts due to the limited opportunities afforded Asian American actors. But he found one in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.”


	Directed by Bassam Tariq and hitting theaters Sept. 25, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” stars two-time Oscar winner Mahershala Ali as Latif, a devout Muslim hitman in Houston, Texas, forced to go on the run with his three children — including a baby boy — when he runs afoul of his employer and a fanatical, heavily-armed Christian pastor Hwan (Cho), whose flock has declared holy war on porn. Sporting a cowboy hat, grill and goatee, Cho makes for a menacing villain who more than holds his own against the heavyweight Ali. It’s his finest performance in years and proof that he can go to deep, dark places if given the chance.
	

	In a wide-ranging conversation with Variety, Cho discussed his Hollywood journey.
	
		What was it like to finally play the villain? It looks like you had fun.	

	I knew how people saw me and what my filmography was and what people know me for, so I wanted to not distract from the film. I wanted to be in the movie and not taking anyone’s attention away from the story. I was really anxious about concentrating on the work and going as deep as I possibly could with Mahershala. I knew that this would be a singular challenge for me and wanted to do Mahershala justice because I’m such an admirer of his.
	
		This is a very soulful film that humanizes the Muslim experience in America. What was it like to play a part in that? Because this is a very underrepresented community onscreen.	

	Thanks for asking that. I’m from an underrepresented community also cinematically, so it felt right to help tell an underrepresented story. It felt good and it felt gratifying to be invited to assist in that storytelling. What I related to from the Muslim experience — from Latif’s experience — was the ardent nature of faith. If there was one obstacle I wanted to clear up early with Bassam, it was: “We’re not making fun of Pastor Hwan, correct?” I needed to play him like he really believes his own words and his followers believe what he’s saying. Ardent faith can result in good things and bad outcomes as well, and that’s where I found commonality.
	
		“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” is being released at a time where Israel and Palestine are dominating the news and there is a lot of Islamophobia being bandied about. To have a film like this come out that presents a loving portrait of a Muslim American family feels very timely.	

	What I think is really important and am gratified to see is the humanization of Muslims in this moment. I am personally surprised by how much Islamophobia there is and how explicit it is. If there’s anything we ought to do to tell any story it’s to humanize people and I’m happy to be a part of that.



	

					John Cho as Pastor Hwan and Mahershala Ali as Latif in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.”
									Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios
	


	
		Were you and other folks on set keenly aware that this was essentially Bassam and Mahershala finally getting to make their “Blade” film? Because they’d been trying to make a “Blade” movie forever and I think they got to make an even better version than any that could have happened under the Marvel umbrella.	

	If you can believe it — because I feel really stupid saying the following — I was not aware! By the time I was cast and we started rehearsals, we were in a moving vehicle that was going very fast. I’m finding out more about the origins of the story through articles and doing press. They’d talked about working on “Blade” together and alluded to a history, but I was of the mindset of: “If this isn’t helping us right now this isn’t my business because we need to make a movie.”
	
	
		Pastor Hwan’s whole deal is he conflates consensual pornography with sex trafficking, which seems to be a prevalent issue these days.	

	It almost passed by me on the first read, like, “Oh, he’s not seeing this correctly.” I’ll say an observation that I have noted for myself in these last few years: On the one hand, there’s more porn ever being produced and it’s more accessible than it ever was; and on this parallel track, you have this growing obsession with trafficking people. One is consensual, theoretically, and one is not. Those two things have grown together and they’re not explicitly connected; you know what I mean? I would say that the general reaction to the Epstein Files is reflective of some of the confusion in our country regarding: What is trafficking, really?
	
		How did your Christian upbringing influence your portrayal of Pastor Hwan? Your father was a minister in the Church of Christ, which is pretty strict, right?	

	It is. There are different denominations and I don’t want to speak out of turn, but it is fundamentalist. It felt very normal to me growing up and did not bear a cosmetic resemblance to Hwan and his church. The thing that I took from that experience for the role was conceiving of Hwan as someone who, even though his actions are megalomaniacal, he thinks he’s a servant. And those are the kinds of pastors I grew up with: People who believe they were in service to their congregation.

	Houston was the first place we immigrated to from Korea, so playing Pastor Hwan touched a lot of nerves for me. Let’s say we landed in America when I was six, and started going to church, and we’re in Houston — how does [Hwan] get here? But it was pleasurable also to return to Houston wearing a cowboy hat in this marvelous action package. I didn’t quite see it coming but this kind of tickled the boy that immigrated from Korea to Houston.
	
		I read that the Church of Christ rejects instruments and performs music a cappella. And you have a big a cappella performance in this movie where you’re singing a hymn to your flock while wielding a machine gun.	

	It was very natural to go into an a cappella performance and sing, and my first day on set was doing that scene and singing to the people. Mahershala was shocked that that was my first scene and I could walk right into that, but I think it was my upbringing where I could walk right into that and say, “Yeah, let’s go.” I got plopped right in!
	


	
		I’m half-Korean, so I’m curious what it was like for you as a Korean American actor and an Asian actor trying to break into Hollywood in the ‘90s and early aughts? As a viewer, it seemed like you were one of the only ones out there.	

	I didn’t grow up wanting to be an actor or even conceiving that that was possible. I just assumed that a lot of the Asian actors on television were amateurs or something — like. when they needed an Asian actor, they’d get somebody from the bank to come in. I didn’t realize that they were professionals that went to acting school, moved to L.A. or New York, and got agents. All of it seemed so far beyond the realm of possibility for me, so I was on an island.

	The reason I decided to become an actor was I did a play in college [“The Woman Warrior”] where I met all these other Asian American actors and found a community. The thing that I struggled with and continue to struggle with — even in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” — is that the lack of cinematic vocabulary for Asian American actors makes it hard to imagine bigger and makes it hard to conceive of other ideas. I never had that library that I could pull from in my mind, so I thought, “What am I supposed to do?” “How am I supposed to navigate this?!” It felt very lonesome at times. It doesn’t feel as lonesome anymore.
	
		I’ve spoken with Randall Park about this, but what was your experience like reading for roles in the ‘90s and early 2000s? Was it a lot of racist Asian stereotypes with accents?	

	Sure. I remember those first few years back when network television was a thing, right around November you’d get an audition for the show’s “Chinatown” episode. That was when, as a young Asian man, you’d maybe get an audition. But I was never good for that! I never looked like the tough guy, so I was going down a gangplank there. I got my leather jacket from the thrift store and tried to look tough, but it never really worked!

	I do remember very clearly doing a role early on where I was a Chinese delivery boy who had a Southern accent and that was a laugh because he didn’t have a Chinese accent. It was for “The Jeff Foxworthy Show,” and I remember standing there and seeing everyone laugh and thinking, “I don’t want to do this. This is not worth it, whatever I’m getting paid.” I didn’t like that laugh. I remember feeling something in me, and so I tried to say no to those auditions going forward because I didn’t want to be in that position again.
	
	
		Looking back on those early days, did it even seem feasible to you that you’d become a leading man one day?	

	It’s complicated, because you try not to think about it, but you also have to dream. For a time, in the late- ‘90s, it seemed like some progress could happen if the independent filmmakers broke through. It wasn’t the revolution exactly that we wanted, but there was that strain of hope on the independent side. I tried not to think about it too far, and maybe that was a trick that I was doing for myself. But it didn’t seem within reach or logical.
	
		In 2015, you tweeted, “Stop turning Asian roles white. It’s bullshit and we all know it.” I believe this was around the time of Scarlett Johansson being cast as the lead in “Ghost in the Shell,” but what prompted you to write that?	

	I can’t exactly recall. At the time, it felt like, “I have this much on my plate and you’re taking that off my plate. I have three ribs on my plate, and now I have two ribs, and now I have one rib.” It felt like that. When you’re in an environment of diminished resources, you get hangry. I was also thinking about Asian-themed films that were being helmed by white characters, which seemed illogical. There were a lot of things I was thinking about.



	

					John Cho as Pastor Hwan and Mahershala Ali as Latif in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.”
									Jaclyn Martinez
	


	
		The following year, the viral #StarringJohnCho campaign happened where your face was superimposed onto movie posters to highlight the lack of Asian American representation in Hollywood. How did you feel about that?	

	Even though it bears my name, I feel distanced from it because it wasn’t my idea. Though I know the creator Will [Yu], he didn’t ask for my permission and then it had a life of its own that didn’t involve me. I admired it, but I was also embarrassed about it to some degree. It felt like I was taking an ad out in Variety! You know what I mean? And I wasn’t doing that. I’m just over here working. I don’t think it was the intention, but it also suggested: “Give this guy a handout over here!” And I was like, I’m good, I’m over here working and doing my best. I would say, at the end of the day, I’m glad the discussion was had and you might as well use me as a point of initiation, but yes, it was odd!
	
	
		The fact that the #StarringJohnCho viral campaign inspired Jon M. Chu to adapt “Crazy Rich Asians” into a movie is pretty wild.	

	That part is wild. Jon told me that and I didn’t know. If I had read that in an article, I might have raised an eyebrow and not believed him, but it’s authentic and for that single reason it was worth it.
	
		One thing that kind of infuriated me as a Korean American was how none of the actors in “Parasite” were nominated for major awards or were even in the conversation for them. It served as a major example of how Asian actors are overlooked — that you can award behind-the-scenes people on a film but not those in front of the camera.	

	I was at the Oscars the year “Parasite” won, and I remember walking to the Governors Ball and somebody — I don’t remember who it was — shaking my hand very vigorously and saying, “Congratulations!” You draw up the conclusion you will from that. But with the Oscars, I don’t track that very seriously for myself because with the history of the Oscars, I think about all my favorite movies and actors and go, “Oh my god! Miss, miss, miss!” There are a lot of misses in Oscar history and they’re very personal to me because a lot of my favorite films and performances have been misses.

	What I will say is: Mainstream culture, especially with representation and especially as it relates to Asian representation, has always wanted to declare it “over” and say, “Are we there now?” “Is this enough?” And for me, it’s not about whether we’ve had enough accolades; it’s an ongoing process of people being allowed to participate in this tradition. Are we excluded or included? I do see a lot of good signs underneath, which is filmmakers, showrunners and writers working at a high level. We didn’t’ have that infrastructure in the ‘90s. That, to me, is encouraging.
	
		The lack of Asian representation in Hollywood studio movies has always rankled me because more than half the box office for a blockbuster movie comes from Asia, so it would even financially behoove studios to cast an Asian actor in their big studio movie and yet it still doesn’t happen all that often.	

	I suspect you’re reading my diary based on what you just said! I’ve had the same thought as well. What is preventing you from seeing very easy math? When a movie is being conceived, it’s usually the question of: How can we convince this individual to gamble this amount of dollars? And those individuals are not necessarily doing great vetting. It’s really about the people who write checks and what their makeup is. But I share your frustration. And not recognizing Asian actors is also curious. We’re still dealing with a layer where people are not conferring 100% humanity on a lot of Asian American performers. When I got my start in the ‘90s, there was a very explicit belief that Asians were not capable of being funny, so it was hard to get auditions for comedic roles — unless you were the butt of the joke.
	



	

					John Cho and Kal Penn in “Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle.” 
									©New Line Cinema/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		As a fan of the “Harold & Kumar” films, I’d be remiss if I didn’t ask you about what’s going on with “Harold & Kumar 4.”	

	That would be fun and I can confirm that it is allegedly gestating with me and Kal Penn. We’re older and if we do this, I think it would be really interesting because I can’t believe how many fundamental things have changed in the time we’ve done these movies! The headliner is that weed is legal. The movies talk about cultural politics and national politics and everything there has also changed, so I think it would be interesting to see what this movie would be.
	
		The first time I saw you onscreen was in “American Pie” as “MILF Guy #2.” What are your thoughts when you look back on playing “MILF Guy #2?” And have you ever met Jennifer Coolidge, and was that awkward for you?	

	I have met Jennifer Coolidge, and it was not awkward in the least! She’s lovely! Let that be the headline. But I haven’t worked with her; I’ve only talked… about her. I didn’t know what I was getting into. The movie is so sweet and unassuming in its own way, and it spawned all these Xerox copies of “American Pie” in the ensuing years, but they only copied the raunchiness. It felt small, and I was away for the summer it was released, and when I came back to town it was just people chanting, “MILF! MILF!” at me all the time. At that age, I was not equipped to handle what that was — people laughing and pointing and high-fiving. And people still recognize me from that one line in the movie, if you can believe it. It was my first experience with notoriety, and I was not prepared for that.
	
		It’s funny that you helped popularize the term “MILF,” which is a popular category of porn, and in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” you are going to war on porn.	

	Yeah! Maybe I willed it to happen. I’m killing my younger self.
	
		I wanted to ask you about the Quentin Tarantino “Star Trek” movie that never came to fruition. From what I understand, it was based on the “Star Trek” episode “A Piece of Action” that’s set on a 1920s gangster planet, and Tarantino described it as “‘Pulp Fiction’ in space.”	

	Ugh. I’m actually entering a deep depression right now that it didn’t happen. At the time I’d heard rumors, and Simon [Pegg] is way more inside of it and was privy to information that I was not. I heard that Quentin Tarantino was interested and there was a pitch, but the details were not relayed to me. Was I crossing fingers underneath a desk? Oh yeah. I can see why people might have paused. Are we making a “Star Trek” movie or just using “Star Trek” to make a Quentin Tarantino movie? It’s a legitimate question, but I just wanted to make a Quentin Tarantino movie. That would have been a dream.

schema.headline: John Cho’s Odyssey From ‘MILF Guy #2’ to Porn-Hating Pastor in ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’: ‘It Felt Very Lonesome at Times’

title: Montclair Film Festival Sets 2026 Lineup With ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘I Play Rocky,’ ‘The Debut’ and More (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The Montclair Film Festival has unveiled the complete lineup for its 2026 edition, bringing a slate of international premieres, awards season conten
body:
The Montclair Film Festival has unveiled the complete lineup for its 2026 edition, bringing a slate of international premieres, awards season contenders, documentaries and independent films to New Jersey.

	Among the highlights are Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s “La Bola Negra,” Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” Sian Heder’s “Being Heumann,” James Gray’s “Paper Tiger” and Mike Leigh’s “Tender Loving Care.”
	

	The festival will also feature appearances from Tim Blake Nelson, Edward Burns, Jesse Eisenberg, Susie Essman, Paul Giamatti, Stephan James, Karina Longworth, Rachel Maddow, Julianne Moore and John Turturro. They join previously announced honorees Beth de Araújo, Stephen Beresford, Ava DuVernay, Tony Gilroy and Jack O’Connell.


	The festival will open Oct. 16 with Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine” at the Wellmont Theater, and will close with Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” on Oct. 25 at MKA Upper School. The centerpiece selections include Ava DuVernay’s documentary “14th,” Simon Stone’s drama “Elsinore” and Brad Bird’s animated feature “Ray Gunn.”

	Several of the festival’s most prominent events will feature filmmakers and stars in person. Eisenberg will join Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore for a conversation about “The Debut,” moderated by Stephen Colbert. Edward Burns will attend a screening of “Beneath the Blue Suburban Skies,” while Nelson will appear for “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd.” John Turturro will participate in a Q&A following “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” and Susie Essman will attend a screening of “The Good Life.”
	

	The festival’s 2026 David Carr Award for Truth in Non-Fiction Filmmaking will go to director Ben Klein and producer Rachel Maddow for “Kill. Bury. Print.,” which examines an escalating conflict between a community newspaper and the sheriff of the Oklahoma county it covers. Klein and Maddow will participate in a post-screening Q&A.

	The festival will also present juried competitions in documentary, fiction and Future/Now, the latter honoring emerging independent filmmakers with the $5,000 Mark Urman Award. Documentary contenders include “Closure,” “The Great Experiment,” “One in a Million,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution” and “When a Witness Recants.” The fiction competition features “All of a Sudden,” “Fatherland,” “Minotaur,” “Possible Love” and “Rose.”

	The short-film competitions will include documentary, fiction and New Jersey categories, with selections ranging from Ben Proudfoot and Stephen Curry’s “The Baddest Speechwriter of All” to “Albatross,” “Callback,” “Scratch,” “St. Joseph” and “Us Being Epic.”

	Other programming includes panels on new pathways into filmmaking, the New Jersey film and television industry, festival programming and the relationship between box office and awards momentum. 

	Tickets go on sale Sept. 28 at 10 a.m. for Montclair Film members and Oct. 1 at 10 a.m. for the public.

	The complete lineup of films is below. The festival runs from Oct. 16-25.

	In Conversation

	In Conversation With Stephan JamesSunday, Oct. 18, 6:30 p.m., Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine

	In Conversation With Karina LongworthSunday, Oct. 25, noon, Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine

	Panels

	Inside Puppet Heap: Fabrication in FilmmakingGo behind the scenes with Puppet Heap, the award-winning studio behind dozens of original films, TV productions and iconic puppet creations. Screenings of Puppet Heap’s original short films, narrated by the studio’s larger-than-life mascot, the Heap, show audiences how puppets are designed, built and brought to life for the camera. The presentation features production puppets, fabrication insights and techniques, plus a live Q&A. Recommended for ages 10 and up.Sunday, Oct. 18, 1 p.m., Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine

	Who Gets to Make Movies Now? New Paths, New VoicesThe path to becoming a filmmaker is evolving in disruptive and exciting ways. Today’s emerging talent comes from an increasingly wide range of backgrounds: not just film schools or traditional industry jobs, but online communities, independent production, other creative disciplines and entirely unexpected places. Christopher Rosen, deputy editor at The Ankler and co-host of the “Prestige Junkie” podcast, leads a panel of creators and entertainment stakeholders. They explore the new routes into filmmaking, the perspectives fresh voices bring to the screen and what these changing pathways mean for how the industry discovers, develops and champions the next generation of big-screen storytellers. Presented in partnership with The Ankler.Sunday, Oct. 18, 4 p.m., Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine

	Art Can Save Our Democracy: How Creativity Can Be a Force for GoodLaw professor, writer and human rights advocate Alan Jenkins leads a panel of local arts leaders on the vital role the arts play in defending democracy. Panelists from Montclair organizations including the Montclair Art Museum, Jazz House Kids, Vanguard Theater Group and Montclair Film discuss how artists and cultural institutions fight injustice, inspire civic engagement and address global issues in their own community.Monday, Oct. 19, 7 p.m., Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine

	Breaking Into the Business: Your Guide to New Jersey’s Film and Television IndustryIndustry veterans and film commissioners discuss how to break into New Jersey’s growing film and TV industry. The conversation highlights resources including NJ 411, the Actors Hub, Film Ready New Jersey and the Take 2 program. Panelists also share practical guidance on identifying legitimate opportunities, avoiding common pitfalls and building meaningful industry connections. Presented in partnership with the New Jersey Economic Development Authority and the New Jersey Motion Picture and Television Commission.Thursday, Oct. 22, 6 p.m., Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine
	

	Meet the ProgrammersMallory Martin, executive director of Film Festival Alliance, hosts programmers from Montclair and other visiting festivals. They take filmmakers inside the process of selecting films for festivals, with insights, tips and an open dialogue on building a program. Presented in partnership with Film Festival Alliance.Saturday, Oct. 24, 10 a.m., Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine

	Box Office, Buzz and the Race AheadThis year’s most talked-about movies are bringing big, enthusiastic audiences back to theaters and reshaping the awards conversation along the way. They range from blockbusters such as “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to indie breakouts such as “Obsession” and “The Invite.” As box office momentum, new creator pipelines and evolving business models collide with critical acclaim, industry buzz and Oscar ambition, what does commercial success mean for a film’s awards prospects now? Katey Rich, awards editor at The Ankler and host of the “Prestige Junkie” podcast, leads a panel of film insiders and awards experts. They unpack the season’s biggest contenders, the performances and filmmakers breaking through and how a resurgent theatrical marketplace could shape the race to Oscar night. Presented in partnership with The Ankler.Sunday, Oct. 25, 4 p.m., Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine

	Special Events

	StorySlam: Scary Stories for the ScreenFan-favorite storytellers from past events return for a special Montclair Film Festival StorySlam, sharing coming-of-age stories around the theme “Feeling Fifteen.” Expect an evening of laughter and emotion.Wednesday, Oct. 21, 7:30 p.m., Audible Lounge at Montclair Mezzanine

	Montclair Improv ComedyVeterans of some of the best improv theaters bring an original night of comedy, courtesy of Montclair Improv Comedy.Thursday, Oct. 22, 7:30 p.m., Cinema505

	Meet Us on Church StreetFree, family-friendly live events and activities throughout the day, presented with Montclair’s Complete Streets. More information will be available on the Montclair Film website in early October.Saturday, Oct. 24, Church Street

title: ‘Evil Dead Burn’ Sets HBO Max Release Date in Time for Halloween
description:
One of the year’s scariest movies will be ready to stream before Halloween: “Evil Dead Burn” will be released on HBO Max on Oct. 2.

	The third movi
body:
One of the year’s scariest movies will be ready to stream before Halloween: “Evil Dead Burn” will be released on HBO Max on Oct. 2.

	The third movie since the “Evil Dead” series reboot in 2013 (and sixth film in the franchise overall) had its theatrical release July 10. Directed by Sébastien Vaniček, “Evil Dead Burn” stars Souheila Yacoub (“Dune: Part Two”) as a woman looking for comfort from her in-laws after her husband’s death. Their gathering at a secluded house quickly turns into a hellish reunion as the family members turn into Deadites. 
	

	The film also stars Hunter Doohan (“Wednesday,” “Daredevil: Born Again”), Luciane Buchanan (“The Night Agent”), Tandi Wright (“Pearl”), Erroll Shand (“Chief of War”), George Pullar (“It Only Takes a Night”) and Maude Davey (”The Newsreader”). 


	The “Evil Dead” horror franchise was created by Sam Raimi that now spans six films and a television series. The franchise follows various characters as they face demonic entities known as Deadites, raised with the help of a strange book of the dead (known as the Naturom Demonto in movies one, four and five, and as the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis in movies two, three and six). 

	The original trilogy starred Bruce Campbell in “The Evil Dead” (1981), “Evil Dead II” (1987) and “Army of Darkness” (1992). The franchise continued with the 2013 standalone sequel “Evil Dead.” Campbell reprised his role in a Starz television series, “Ash vs Evil Dead,” which ran from 2015-2018. The fifth film in the franchise, “Evil Dead Rise,” was released in 2023. A seventh film, “Evil Dead Wrath,” helmed by Francis Galluppi, is slated for an April 2028 release.
	

	Raimi and Robert Tapert produced under their Ghost House Pictures banner. Campbell, Romel Adam, Lee Cronin and Jose Cañas executive produced.

body:
Kaia Gerber
                          Missing Cat Is Found!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 25, 2026
                            8:31 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
            Kaia Gerber's cat that went missing this past week has been found ... and apparently her friends' efforts helped reunite the pet with its celeb owner.
      
    
            A source tells TMZ ... the model's cat, Tony, was found Thursday via a tracker.
      
    
            As we reported ... Kaia's friends Jake Shane, Lewis Pullman and Carissa Gallo were spotted posting missing cat flyers all around the Hollywood Hills.
      

            The posters -- which listed a reward for the "LOST CAT" -- pointed out that the feline could easily be ID'd by his tracker.
      
    
            Her friends' sweet gestures come in the wake of the death of her brother Presley Gerber -- who was found dead in his room inside a Santa Monica sober living facility Sunday after a suspected overdose.

title: Laura Dern Brings Gifts to Former Costar Kaia Gerber's House After Presley's Death
description:
Laura Dern
                          I'm Showing Up For Kaia Gerber ...
body:
Laura Dern
                          I'm Showing Up For Kaia Gerber ...
                          And I Come Bearing Gifts
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 25, 2026
                            8:20 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kaia Gerber is receiving support from Hollywood royalty during a trying time ... with Laura Dern showing up at her home ... and she wasn't empty-handed.
      
    
            The legendary actress was spotted grabbing goodie bags and a flower bouquet from her car outside Kaia's Los Angeles-area home ... paying a visit as the model mourns her brother Presley's death.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Laura wore a black sweater and blue jeans to see her friend.
      

            If you didn't know ... Laura has a longstanding relationship with Kaia's mom, Cindy Crawford.
      
    
            Kaia and Laura have worked together too ... starring in the AppleTV+ show "Palm Royale" together.
      
    
            As we reported, it's been a terrible week for Kaia ... her brother was found dead in a Santa Monica rehab facility on Sunday in what authorities suspect may be a drug overdose.
      
    
            Days after Presley's death, Kaia's cat ran away ... just another thing going wrong during what was already a difficult time.
      
    
            Hopefully Laura's visit boosted her spirits.

title: R&B Singer Keke Wyatt Arrested for Terroristic Threats and Cruelty to Children
description:
R&B Star Keke Wyatt
                          Wild Arrest In Georgia ...
body:
R&B Star Keke Wyatt
                          Wild Arrest In Georgia ...
                          Over Alleged Assault, Threats & Child Cruelty
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 25, 2026
                            7:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            R&B sensation Keke Wyatt must be singing the blues ... after getting arrested in Georgia on 3 serious offenses, TMZ has learned
      
    
            A rep for the Henry County Sheriff's Office tells TMZ ... Keke was busted September 20 and then booked into the Henry County jail for terroristic threats, simple assault, and cruelty to children.
      
    
            The sheriff says Keke was released two days later after posting a $1,050 bond. We're working on getting details on what Keke allegedly did to get tossed in the clink.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Keke is well known for her R&B music and rose to national fame in the early 2000s after her duets with singer Avant became huge hits. The songs, "My First Love" and "Nothing in This World," appear on her gold record, "Soul Sista."
      
    
            She also starred on all 3 seasons of TV One's popular reality show, "R&B Divas: Atlanta" and "Keke Wyatt's World."
